note_on_method: Each venue page rests on one City of Spokane page - the Recreational Fields and Sports page, whose "Tennis and Pickleball Courts" section lists every park with a court, a street address and a count - plus the US Census address geocoder for the county and the postcode. The City's page cannot be fetched by a script, because my.spokanecity.org answers every scripted request with a redirect into a "Checking Your Browser" interstitial, so it was read in a browser on 7 September 2026 and saved as text, and every quoted line is asserted against that file on every build. Where the City is silent, these pages record the silence.

slots.description:
Two pickleball courts striped on the two tennis courts at A.M. Cannon Park, in the West Central neighbourhood north of the river.

The City counts this park twice, once on each of two lists, and the two counts are the same. Its "Tennis Courts Striped for Pickleball" list reads "A.M. Cannon Park, 1511 N. Elm St., 2 Courts", and its "Tennis Courts" list reads the same park with the same "2 Courts". That is one pickleball court to a tennis court - a different arrangement from Comstock, Mission and Peaceful Valley, where the City's pickleball number is twice its tennis number. So the two pickleball courts here are the two tennis courts, shared with tennis, not lined side by side across them.

This is the one Spokane venue the imported dataset this site was built from had no row for at all. The City's line minted it: a name, an address that resolves, a count. Nothing else about the park is stated on the page - no hours, no lighting, no surface, no nets, no price - and this page does not add anything the City has not written.
slots.getting_there:
1511 N Elm St, Spokane, WA 99201.

The City writes the street with a full stop after the type, "1511 N. Elm St."; the Census address geocoder matched it as written, at house-number level, and placed it in Spokane County, in the incorporated place Spokane. The park is in the West Central neighbourhood, north of the river.

The City publishes nothing about parking at this park, nothing about transit and nothing about where the courts sit inside it. There is no lot described, no capacity and no fee, and this site does not read a lot off a map.
slots.what_to_expect:
Two courts, which is one game at a time, and a wait if a game is on when you arrive. Because the pickleball courts and the tennis courts are the same two slabs, a tennis match takes half the venue and two of them take all of it.

The rule for getting on is the City's one sentence for every court in the section: "Tennis & Pickleball courts are first-come-first-served, however if you would like to officially reserve a court and receive a reservation permit please fill out the online form." Turning up is the normal way in; a permit is the other, and the City publishes no price, no lead time and no calendar for it. The section's introduction says the City's tennis courts "host neighborhood pick-up games, parks and recreation classes and many tennis events", so a class or an event here is a class or an event on the pickleball courts.

The City states no hours and no lighting, so this page cannot tell you whether an evening game is possible. It names no surface and says nothing about nets, so bring your own if you can. It never writes "outdoor" against any court on the page, so neither indoor nor outdoor is recorded here.

faqs.a: Two pickleball courts, striped on the park's two tennis courts. The City's striped list reads "A.M. Cannon Park, 1511 N. Elm St., 2 Courts", and its tennis list gives the same park two courts.

faqs.q: Are the courts dedicated to pickleball?
faqs.a: No. They are the tennis courts, striped for pickleball and shared with tennis. One pickleball court to a tennis court here, where Comstock and Mission have two.
Not stated. The City says the courts are first-come-first-served and can be officially reserved with a reservation permit by online form; it publishes no price and never says the courts are free.

faqs.q: Are the courts lit, and what are the hours?
faqs.a: Neither is stated. The City's section carries no hours and no lighting for any park, so both read as not verified here.

faqs.q: Why was this park not in the original dataset?
faqs.a: The imported dataset had no row for A.M. Cannon Park. The City's line supplied a name, an address that resolves and a count, and that is enough to publish.

slots.description:
Twelve pickleball courts striped on the six tennis courts at Comstock Park on the South Hill, the second-largest set in Spokane.

The City's two lists give the two numbers that describe this venue. "Tennis Courts Striped for Pickleball" reads "Comstock Park, 601 W. 29th Ave., 12 Courts"; "Tennis Courts" reads "Comstock Park, 601 W. 29th Ave., 6 Courts". Two pickleball courts to a tennis court, on six slabs, shared with tennis. Twelve is the City's pickleball number and it publishes as stated; six is the number of courts you are sharing.

This is the venue where the City's page changed the record most. The imported dataset this site was built from held Comstock at four courts and at "3012 S Howard St"; the City says twelve at 601 W 29th Ave, and Howard Street and 29th Avenue bound the same park. Both the count and the address were overridden by the City's line, and because the count moved from four to twelve the venue is flagged for a re-check at the next cadence. Nothing else about the park is stated: no hours, no lighting, no surface, no nets, no price.

slots.what_to_expect:
Twelve courts if nobody is playing tennis, and fewer by two for every tennis match under way, because each tennis court carries two pickleball courts. The City publishes no schedule for either sport, so how many of the twelve are yours is decided on arrival.

Access is the City's one sentence for every court in the section: "Tennis & Pickleball courts are first-come-first-served, however if you would like to officially reserve a court and receive a reservation permit please fill out the online form." No price for the permit, no lead time and no calendar are published, so a court under permit is something you find out about when you get there. The City's introduction to the section says its tennis courts "host neighborhood pick-up games, parks and recreation classes and many tennis events", and with six tennis courts this is a park where that sentence is likely to matter.

Hours are not stated. Lighting is not stated. Surface is not stated, and nets are not mentioned for any court on the page. The City never writes "outdoor" against any of its courts, so neither indoor nor outdoor is recorded here, whatever six tennis courts on the South Hill suggest.

Sixteen pickleball courts striped on the eight tennis courts at Mission Park in the Logan neighbourhood, the largest set in Spokane.

The City's striped list reads "Mission Park, 1208 E. Mission Ave., 16 Courts" and its tennis list "Mission Park, 1208 E. Mission Ave., 8 Courts": two pickleball courts to a tennis court, on eight slabs, shared with tennis. Sixteen is the City's pickleball number and it publishes as stated. It is also the largest court count at any verified venue in Washington, and it is a stripe count - the number of pickleball courts that exist when no tennis is being played on any of the eight.

The imported dataset this site was built from held the same address and the same count, so the City's line confirmed the record rather than changing it. What it did change was the note on cost: the dataset said "Free public play", the City says nothing about price, and nothing is what now stands. No hours, no lighting, no surface and no nets are stated for the park.

With eight tennis courts this is the park in Spokane where the City's own description of its tennis courts - they "host neighborhood pick-up games, parks and recreation classes and many tennis events" - has the most room to apply, and a tennis event on eight courts is sixteen pickleball courts you cannot use.

The way on is the City's one sentence for every court: "Tennis & Pickleball courts are first-come-first-served, however if you would like to officially reserve a court and receive a reservation permit please fill out the online form." Turning up is the default. A permit is the alternative, and the City publishes no price, no lead time and no calendar for it, so a reserved court is not something you can check before you leave.

The City states no hours and no lighting, so whether the sixteen are usable after work is not on the record. It names no surface, mentions no nets, and never writes "outdoor" against any court on the page. A count this size with nothing else stated is the shape of the whole Spokane record: a number, an address, and silence.

That one tennis court is a tennis court and is not counted here; the two published are the two the City calls pickleball. Unlike the four striped venues in Spokane, a tennis match at Corbin does not take a pickleball court away.

The imported dataset this site was built from held the park at "501 West Park Place", another side of the same oval; the City's address replaces it. The dataset's note on cost read "Public", which is not a price, and the City writes none either. No hours, no lighting, no surface and no nets are stated for the park.
